name: Combustible gas leak detectors and explosive gas alarms
summary: Handheld sniffers with a gooseneck probe that tick faster near a fuel-gas leak, and plug-in home alarms that sound when natural gas or propane builds up.
uses: Finds leaks of natural gas, propane, butane and petrol vapour at joints, valves, hoses and cylinders; UEi rates its sniffers at under 50 ppm of methane (UEI CD100A, UEI CD200)
Sniffers also react to alcohol, solvents, thinners, ammonia and refrigerants, so a hit doesn't tell you which gas it is (UEI CD100A, UEI CD200)
UEi says its CD100A should not be used to detect carbon monoxide (UEI CD100A); a combined home alarm has a separate CO sensor (KIDDE COPDLG-CA)
Leak finders, not air monitors: Fieldpiece says its heated-diode wand is not a safety device for monitoring fuel-gas levels (FIELDPIECE DRX3)
Home alarms are made to sound before 10% LEL of natural gas or propane; place them where the gas collects, high for natural gas and low for propane (KIDDE COPDLG-CA, KIDDE CA PAGE)
Don't rely on smell alone: the odorant in natural gas and propane can fade, so a nose can miss a leak (NIOSH ODOR FADE)
identify: Handheld sniffers: a small body with a flexible gooseneck about 40 to 50 cm long, a speaker that ticks faster near gas, a sensitivity wheel and LEDs (UEI CD100A, UEI CD200). UEi's sniffers use a solid-state semiconductor sensor (UEI CD100A, UEI CD200); Fieldpiece's DRX3 uses a heated diode and finds natural gas, propane and butane as well as refrigerants (FIELDPIECE DRX3). Many give no number: on a CD100A you set a slow tick in clean air and the tick rises as gas increases (UEI CD100A). Some add an alarm set as a share of methane's LEL (UEI CD200). Scale: 50 ppm methane is 0.1% of the LEL, since methane's LEL is 5% gas in air (MSA 4XR), so a fast tick means a leak to fix, not proof the room is about to explode. Explosion marks such as Class I Division 2 or ATEX Zone 2 appear on some (FIELDPIECE DRX3); UEi says its CD200 is designed not to make sparks, but that the place you use it may have no such safeguards (UEI CD200). Home alarms: plug-in boxes labelled explosive gas, natural gas or propane, often combined with CO. Kidde's COPDLG-CA uses a metal oxide gas sensor, works from 4.4 to 37.8 °C, isn't approved for RVs or boats, meets CSA 6.19 and UL 1484, and chirps for replacement 7 years after it is first powered (KIDDE COPDLG-CA).
test: Switch a sniffer on in clean outdoor air: UEi's CD100A takes the air it starts in as its background level, so start in fresh air; it needs 10 seconds to 2 minutes to settle, the CD200 one minute (UEI CD100A, UEI CD200). UEi's CD200 manual calls for a quick functional test each time it goes into service: expose the sensor to a known leak, like a cigarette lighter's gas, or pass the probe over a drop of combustible fluid; the tick should rise (UEI CD200). That is UEi's check for its own sniffer, not for home alarms or other makers' gear. Do it outdoors with no flame near, release the lighter's gas unlit, and keep the sensor dry; UEi advises yearly calibration (UEI CD200). A tick you can't slow means the sensor may need replacing (UEI CD100A); no rise on gas, or a tick that stays fast after warm-up in clean air, are faults to fix before use (UEI CD200). UEi gives the CD100A's sensor a life of more than 3 years (UEI CD100A); heated-diode tips last about 300 hours of use, which some meters count (FIELDPIECE DRX3). Low batteries make results unreliable (UEI CD200); a 9 V sniffer may run only about 5 hours of use per battery (UEI CD100A). Some sniffers react to soap leak solution, so sniff first and soap second (UEI CD100A). Home alarms: the test button only checks the electronics by simulating gas, not the sensor (KIDDE COPDLG-CA). Replace it 7 years after first power-up; on the COPDLG-CA, two chirps with two amber flashes every minute mean end of life (KIDDE COPDLG-CA). It plugs into a 120 V outlet and 2 AA backup cells keep it working in a power cut; no lithium cells (KIDDE COPDLG-CA, KIDDE CA PAGE).

decay.note: UEi rates the CD100A sensor at over 3 years (UEI CD100A); the CD200 runs on 4 AA cells (UEI CD200); heated-diode tips wear out after about 300 hours (FIELDPIECE DRX3); Kidde's home alarm ends its life at 7 years (KIDDE COPDLG-CA).

improvise: A smell of rotten eggs or boiled cabbage at gas appliances, hoses or cylinders means a leak (RBQ GAS), but don't rely on smell alone: the odorant can fade (NIOSH ODOR FADE). To find a leak at a cylinder, hose or fitting: appliance controls off, cylinder or supply valve open, then spray a 50/50 mix of dish soap and water on the hose and every fitting; small bubbles mark the leak. Close the valve, tighten or replace the part, and test again (RBQ GAS). Never use a flame to look for a leak: put out all flames and ignition sources and don't smoke (RBQ GAS). Do the soap test only where you can't smell strong gas (UEI CD200). If the smell is strong indoors, get everyone out, don't flip switches, shut the gas off if you can do it safely, air the place out only if that can't make a spark, and call for help from a safe place (UEI CD200). Natural gas rises and propane sinks (KIDDE CA PAGE), so propane pools in basements, pits and low spots. A bump-tested 4-gas monitor gives a real %LEL danger reading where a sniffer only points to leaks (MSA 4XR). Dangerous: a flame. Not to be trusted: a home alarm past its 7-year end of life, which Kidde says to replace (KIDDE COPDLG-CA).

buildings.loc: Inside RVs and trailers on the lot, low on a wall near the galley; spares in the parts department
Safety aisle beside the CO and smoke alarms; handheld sniffers in plumbing or tools
Boats with propane stoves, by the galley; chandlery shelves
Plugged in low near a propane furnace or water heater, or high near natural-gas appliances
Kitchen wall near the gas line
